Tarry
TAR-ee
verb
Of uncertain first root, probably a blending of the Old English tergan (“to vex, to delay”) with the Old French targer, “to delay, to linger,” from a Late Latin tardicare, from tardus, “slow”; hence to stay, to abide, to wait, to put off going.

Biblical Definition

To tarry is to stay, to abide in a place, to wait rather than go — and in Scripture it is almost always a command laid upon impatient men. Boaz bids Ruth, “Tarry this night” (Rut 3:13), and the waiting woman receives a kinsman-redeemer in the morning. The risen Christ, before He ascended, “commanded them that they should not depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the promise of the Father” (Act 1:4), and the church that tarried ten days in one accord was clothed with power at Pentecost. Habakkuk is given the great rule of the waiting saint: “though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry” (Hab 2:3) — the vision seems slow to the flesh and is never late to God. But the word’s deepest note sounds in Gethsemane, where the Man of Sorrows, whose soul was exceeding sorrowful even unto death, asked of His three, “tarry ye here, and watch with me” (Mat 26:38) — and they slept. Christ tarried in the garden and drank the cup; His disciples could not tarry one hour. So the word divides the flesh from the Spirit. To tarry is not idleness but obedience: it is the creature refusing to run before his God, holding his post until the word comes. The Lord who bade His own tarry for the Spirit bids His church tarry still, watching for His appearing, since He that shall come will come, and will not tarry.

Webster 1828 Definition

To stay; to abide; to wait; to delay going or coming; to linger in expectation.

expand to see more

TARRY, to stay; to abide; to continue in a place.

To wait; to delay going, in expectation of another’s coming or command.

To be slow in coming, as a vision or a promise long deferred (Hab 2:3).

Christ commanded the disciples to tarry in Jerusalem for the Spirit (Act 1:4).

In Gethsemane, to tarry and watch with Christ was the charge the three failed (Mat 26:38).

Key Scripture

Mat 26:38 — "Then saith he unto them, My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death: tarry ye here, and watch with me."

Act 1:4 — "And, being assembled together with them, commanded them that they should not depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the promise of the Father, which, saith he, ye have heard of me."

Hab 2:3 — "For the vision is yet for an appointed time, but at the end it shall speak, and not lie: though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry."

Rut 3:13 — "Tarry this night, and it shall be in the morning, that if he will perform unto thee the part of a kinsman, well; let him do the kinsman's part: but if he will not do the part of a kinsman to thee, then will I do the part of a kinsman to thee, as the LORD liveth: lie down until the morning."

Modern Corruption

A plain word for waiting, and one the age can hardly bear: it recovers the obedience of the saint who will not run before his God.

expand to see more

There is a live misuse here, and it is the impatience of a generation that will not wait for anything. The flesh reckons every delay a denial and every silence a refusal; it must have the answer now, the harvest now, the vision now, and it calls the God who bids it tarry slow. Habakkuk was taught otherwise: though the vision tarry, wait for it, for it will surely come and will not tarry. What seems slow to the creature is exactly punctual with the Creator, who has appointed the time and will not be hurried by our fretting. To tarry is not to do nothing; it is to hold the post until the word comes.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that waiting is a work of obedience, and Gethsemane is its measure. Christ, whose soul was exceeding sorrowful even unto death, asked no great labour of His three — only that they tarry and watch with Him — and they slept while He sweat as it were great drops of blood. The disciples who could not tarry one hour in the garden tarried ten days in the upper room after His command, and were filled with the Spirit. So the LORD teaches His own to stay where He sets them, watching for His appearing, since He that shall come will come and will not tarry.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means to stay, to abide, to wait, to delay going.

expand to see more

Tarry — probably Old English tergan blended with Old French targer, “to delay.”

Behind it stands the Latin tardus, “slow.”

It denotes staying, abiding, waiting rather than going.

Christ bade the disciples tarry for the promise of the Father (Act 1:4).

Though the vision tarry, wait for it: it will not tarry past its hour (Hab 2:3).

Usage

"Tarry ye here, and watch with me — the lightest charge of Gethsemane, and the three could not keep it."

"The church tarried in Jerusalem till she was clothed with power; obedience waited, and Pentecost came."

"Though it tarry, wait for it: what is slow to the flesh is punctual with God."
